Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

issues.item: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Hard to Recall Deliberately' conflicts with 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.' Deliberate retrieval difficulty and very easy verbal access are opposing states and are hard to reconcile as describing the same patient at the same time, especially alongside 'Overwhelm on Recall,' which implies traumatic recall is effortful and dysregulating rather than easy to discuss.

issues.item: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' directly conflicts with 'When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop.' At this severity level and with strong Trigger↔Memory and Memory→Threat links, these two memory items describe opposing levels of accessibility/distress and are hard to reconcile as the same current presentation.

issues.item: Triggers: Authority Commands: Being given orders or instructions
issues.explanation: The trigger set is hard to reconcile with stalking as the index trauma: 'authority commands' and especially 'bicycle' do not show an evident clinical link to the reported trauma, and the profile provides no memory or appraisal content that would make these idiosyncratic triggers understandable.

Threat items emphasize broad interpersonal attack and generic danger vigilance (loud sounds, scanning exits, watching others for harm), which fits assault/combat/fire trauma better than stalking. For stalking, one would expect threat focused more on being followed, approached, monitored, contacted, or found by the perpetrator.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: 'I am a weak person' sits awkwardly with this profile and occupation unless supported by appraisal content about failure to protect oneself or family; here the other appraisals center on permanent damage and fear of going crazy, so the weakness item feels less coherent with the stalking-specific formulation than those items.

vignette: Amir's life was forever altered on a crisp autumn evening two years ago when he discovered his stalker watching him from across the street. The sound of leaves crunching beneath his feet still echoes in his mind, transporting him back to that moment. He remembers feeling an eerie sense of being followed, which had become all too familiar over the preceding months. His stalker's fixation on him began after a chance encounter at a local café; Amir would later realize that this stranger had been meticulously tracking his every move. As a firefighter, Amir was no stranger to danger, but the threat he faced now was insidious and omnipresent. He found himself perpetually on high alert, scanning exits whenever he entered a room or building, searching for potential escape routes should his stalker reappear. Even the sound of sirens, once a familiar comfort, now sent his heart racing as he instinctively watched others around him, searching for signs that they might be a threat. When memories of the stalking surfaced, Amir felt overwhelmed by emotion, unable to verbalize the turmoil brewing inside. He would become withdrawn, struggling to articulate what had happened, leaving his wife, Sara, worried and feeling helpless. Amir's inability to express himself was not merely a matter of finding words; it was as if the experience itself had rendered him mute. The stalking had left an indelible mark on Amir's sense of self. He had come to believe that he was permanently changed for the worse, his confidence shattered by the feeling of being constantly watched and vulnerable. The very reactions that were meant to protect him now made him question his own sanity; he feared going crazy, unable to shake the notion that his heightened state of alertness was a sign of impending madness. Amir's occupation as a firefighter only served to exacerbate these feelings. Every time he responded to an emergency call, the rush of adrenaline triggered memories of being stalked. He began avoiding bike rides with Sara, a once-beloved pastime, fearing that his stalker might be lurking in the shadows, waiting to pounce. The weight of his weakness, or so he perceived it, threatened to consume him. As time passed, Amir's avoidance behaviors took a toll on his relationships and daily life. He became increasingly withdrawn, struggling to connect with Sara and their friends. His performance at work began to suffer, and the fire department's concern for his well-being was palpable. It was only when Amir found himself frozen in fear during a routine call, unable to respond as his training dictated, that he realized he needed help. Amir's decision to seek therapy was not an admission of weakness but rather a desperate attempt to reclaim his life. He hoped to learn how to silence the cacophony of sounds and emotions that haunted him, to find solace in the quiet moments once again. As he sat in the therapist's office, recounting his story, Amir couldn't help but wonder if it was possible to heal, to rediscover the man he was before the stalking began – strong, capable, and free from fear.
